full_text:
The Lagos State Government has urged residents to take precautionary measures against possible extreme heat and associated health risks.
The Commissioner for the Environment and Water Resources, Mr. Tokunbo Wahab, gave the advisory in a statement issued by the ministry’s Director of Public Affairs, Mr. Kunle Adeshina, on Friday, October 30, 2026, in Lagos.
Wahab said the strengthening El Nino climate pattern and transition into the dry season could contribute to unusual temperatures, dry spells, dust and deteriorating air quality.
He, however, noted that the intensity and local impact of these conditions would depend on prevailing weather patterns.
The commissioner said Lagos’ dense population, rapid urbanisation and concentration of heat-absorbing infrastructure could increase residents’ exposure to extreme heat.
He explained that buildings, roads, limited green spaces and inadequate ventilation could intensify temperatures in densely populated neighbourhoods.
Wahab warned that prolonged exposure to excessive heat could cause dehydration, heat exhaustion and heatstroke, with potentially serious health consequences.
He identified children, older persons, pregnant women, outdoor workers, street traders, construction workers and waste handlers as particularly vulnerable.
He added that people with underlying health conditions were also at increased risk.
The commissioner urged families, employers, schools and community leaders to pay special attention to vulnerable groups and provide appropriate protection.
He warned that extreme heat could worsen existing air-quality challenges, particularly during the dry season when dust and haze might increase.
He said increased reliance on petrol and diesel-powered generators during power interruptions could further aggravate local air pollution.
Wahab advised residents to avoid open burning of refuse and adopt environmentally responsible practices to reduce pollution.
He urged residents to drink sufficient water, wear lightweight clothing, seek shaded and ventilated spaces, and avoid strenuous outdoor activities during peak heat periods.
He also called on schools, markets, workplaces and public facilities to provide adequate ventilation, drinking water and shaded areas.
The commissioner advised residents to watch for symptoms of heat-related illnesses, including excessive sweating, dizziness, headaches, weakness, nausea and muscle cramps.
He said affected persons should be moved to cooler environments, given appropriate cooling assistance and taken for medical attention where necessary.
Wahab warned that sudden collapse or loss of consciousness should be treated as a medical emergency requiring immediate attention.
He also advised people with respiratory conditions to limit exposure to dusty environments and follow relevant health and air-quality advisories.
The commissioner called for collaboration among government agencies, health institutions, environmental experts, businesses and community stakeholders to strengthen preparedness.
He urged residents and businesses to protect existing trees, promote tree planting, preserve green spaces and ensure proper waste disposal.
Wahab said the ministry would continue public awareness campaigns and stakeholder engagement to address emerging environmental risks.
He added that the ministry would collaborate with the Nigerian Meteorological Agency, the Lagos State Ministry of Health and the Lagos State Emergency Management Agency.
According to him, the collaboration will strengthen preparedness and response to potential heat-related challenges.
Meanwhile, rising temperatures in Lagos have boosted demand for cold sachet water, bottled water and soft drinks, with traders reporting increased sales.
From Ikeja to Ogba, Costain, Apongbon, Ebutero and Ajegunle, traders say customers are increasingly seeking chilled beverages to cope with the heat.
Interviews reveal how the hot weather is changing drinking habits, boosting businesses and increasing concerns about plastic waste.
Mrs. Bola Ahmed, a shop owner around Computer Village, Ikeja, said her daily sachet water sales had risen from two or three bags to about 15.
Ahmed said sales of bottled water had also doubled, from five to at least 10 packs daily, since the hot weather began.
“I used to sell two sachet water for N50, but it is now three for N100.
“I thank God that I sell around a busy area and I have constant light. Cold water sells like hot cake during this weather,” she said.
She, however, said she was unaware of how customers disposed of the plastic packaging after purchasing the water.
Similarly, Mr. John Amah, a restaurant owner at Nationwide, Ogba, said the heat had created an additional source of income through increased demand for chilled water.
Amah said customers who bought food increasingly requested extra water, prompting him to increase his stock.
“Since the weather became so hot, people request extra water because my water is always chilled to mortuary standards.
“So, I stock more water and make extra gain from there,” he said.
He said a woman regularly visited his restaurant to collect empty plastic bottles, which he gave her because he had no use for them.
At Ebutero Market, a trader, Mrs. Ngozi Kelvin, said demand for soft drinks, sachet water and other beverages had increased considerably.
Kelvin said unreliable electricity supply had compelled her to buy ice blocks to keep drinks chilled for customers.
Another trader at the market, Mrs. Chioma Ngozi, said increased sales had not necessarily translated into higher profits because of rising fuel and generator maintenance costs.
“The power supply is very unreliable, so I have to rely heavily on generators. Fuel prices are high, and whenever fuel costs go up, it eats into my profits,” she said.
An anonymous trader at Ebutero Market said using a solar-powered refrigerator had helped reduce operating costs and improve profits.
At Costain, Mr. Clement Okpara, a beverage seller on Oroku Street, said increased demand for soft drinks and bottled water had necessitated more frequent stock replenishment.
Okpara said he received 35 packs of bottled water on Monday and had sold all the bottles by Friday.
Similarly, Mrs. Oluwafunke Ajiyo, a drink hawker who sourced supplies from Apongbon Market, said her daily bottled water sales had increased from one pack to between three and eight.
Ajiyo said she made about N400 profit per pack, depending on sales.
For consumers, the rising temperatures have also meant spending more on water and adjusting their usual drinking habits.
Miss Eminsule Goodness, a Costain resident, said the heat had increased her consumption of sachet water and cold drinks.
Goodness said five bags of sachet water, previously sold for N1,000, now cost N1,500, adding to her daily expenses.
She said she reused bottled water containers by refilling them for personal use and sold excess plastics for recycling.
Mr. Francis Anyanwu, a civil engineer working in Ijora, Apapa, said he and his colleagues had replaced their usual morning coffee with cold water and soft drinks.
Anyanwu said a pack of bottled water that previously sold for N1,500 now cost N1,800, although the increase had not discouraged his consumption.
Another consumer, Miss Chiamaka Aguse, a resident of Isheri Osun, Ikotun, said she consumed about six sachets of water daily because of the heat.
Aguse said she spent about N200 daily on sachet water, which sold at three sachets for N100.
She said she disposed of used sachets in a waste bin, adding that her personal waste bin was now emptied every three days instead of six.
Miss Divine-Favour Johnson, a Lagos State University student, said she consumed more water during hot weather but preferred carrying reusable bottles from home.
Johnson said her household separated plastics, paper and organic waste for recycling, limiting the additional plastic waste generated by increased water consumption.
While the heat has created opportunities for beverage traders, it has also increased household spending and highlighted the need for responsible plastic waste disposal.
The accounts of traders and consumers show how rising temperatures are influencing everyday choices, from business operations and spending habits to water consumption and waste management.
By Uchechi Afonne, Esther Nwabueze and Mariam Hassan

title: Helicopter sorties were allowed despite orange alert and CMO advice to regulate tourists, says activist - The Hindu

full_text:
Friday’s (October 30, 2026) helicopter crash on the Badrinath-Dehradun route, which killed six people, including the pilot, has brought Uttarakhand’s helicopter safety regulations under fresh scrutiny, particularly the decision to allow flights despite weather warnings issued for the region.
Activist Anoop Nautiyal said the tragedy was particularly disturbing as weather warnings had been issued in advance. An orange alert (for heavy to very heavy rainfall and snowfall) had been issued for five districts, including Chamoli, for October 30.
“A press release issued at 5.44 p.m. on October 29, following a meeting chaired by Disaster Management Secretary Vinod Kumar Suman, had called for heightened vigilance and directed that passengers be moved to safe locations in the event of deteriorating weather,” Mr. Nautiyal said.
He said the Chief Minister’s Office (CMO) had also reiterated these concerns in a communication issued at 8.01 a.m. on October 30, advising authorities to regulate tourist movement in high-altitude areas in view of the orange alert.
“Despite these warnings, helicopter sorties reportedly continued. This raises questions about who authorised the flights, whether the Uttarakhand Civil Aviation Development Authority (UCADA) enforced the necessary restrictions and why commercial operations were allowed to continue under potentially unsafe conditions,” he said.
Series of accidents
The latest crash comes after a series of helicopter accidents during the 2025 Char Dham Yatra. A crash between Kharsali and Jhala on May 8, 2025 killed six people, while an Aryan Aviation helicopter crashed near Gaurikund on June 15, 2025 killing seven. Five helicopter incidents were reported within just 45 days.
The Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau’s (AAIB) probe into the last year’s June crash cited rapidly descending clouds, loss of visual reference, the decision to continue along the route and the pilot’s limited experience in the Kedarnath valley as contributing factors.
In July 2025, the Ministry of Civil Aviation told Parliament that Uttarakhand accounted for more than half of the 12 helicopter accidents reported nationwide since 2020, as well as 21 of the 30 deaths.
Responding to Mr. Nautiyal’s allegations that weather warnings had been ignored, Prateek Jain, the Chief Executive Officer of UCADA, said the agency was following all prescribed safety norms.
“At the time the helicopter crashed, the weather was clear. Two sorties took off before it and two after it, and all of them landed safely,” he said, adding that a detailed investigation into the cause of the accident was under way.
Naveen Singh, a pilgrim from Madhya Pradesh who undertook the Kedarnath Yatra by helicopter this year, questioned whether the corrective measures announced after last year’s accidents had been effectively implemented. “The helicopter I travelled in flew in cloudy weather, but we landed safely,” he said.
High-altitude challenges
Flight operators in Uttarakhand said flying in the Himalayas posed particular operational challenges. Thin air at high altitudes reduces rotor lift and engine power, leaving pilots with less margin for hovering, climbing and carrying passengers.
Despite the risks, helicopter services remain a lucrative part of the pilgrimage economy. More than a dozen companies deploy around 30 single-engine helicopters each season, generating an estimated ₹800 crore annually.
A veteran Kedarnath shuttle pilot, however, said the business was neither as easy nor as profitable as it appeared. He pointed to the absence of radar coverage, dedicated air traffic control, and real-time weather monitoring as major challenges. “Fast-changing mountain weather and the scarcity of emergency landing sites also put passengers and pilots at considerable risk,” he said.

title: Delhi Rain Triggers IMD Red Alert, AQI Improves - Urban Acres

full_text:
Delhi recorded its wettest October day in four years after overnight rain, prompting the India Meteorological Department (IMD) to issue a red alert for more showers, thunderstorms and lightning across the capital on Friday.
The city received 61.4 mm of rainfall in the 24 hours ending at 8.30 am, taking October’s cumulative rainfall to 123.3 mm, according to weather data cited by the IMD. The rainfall also pushed Delhi’s monthly total close to the 128 mm recorded during the whole of October 2022, when the city last saw a higher single-day October rainfall of 74 mm on October 9.
The IMD said light to moderate rain accompanied by thunderstorms and lightning was very likely at most places over the following three hours, with heavy rainfall expected at isolated locations. Its red alert covered southeast Delhi, east Delhi, Shahdara, central Delhi, northeast Delhi, south Delhi, New Delhi, southwest Delhi, west Delhi, northwest Delhi and north Delhi.
The most intense rainfall in the available station-wise data was recorded at Jharoda Kalan, which received 89 mm between 8.30 am on Thursday and 6 am on Friday. Lodi Road recorded 63 mm and Safdarjung, Delhi’s base weather station, received 56.5 mm. Jhajjar recorded 47 mm, Narayana 44.5 mm, Pitampura 42.5 mm and Pusa 41.5 mm.
Other reported totals included 41 mm at Kamla Nehru Nagar in Ghaziabad, 40.9 mm at Pragati Maidan, 36 mm in Gurugram, 35.5 mm in Janakpuri, 35 mm in Muradnagar and 30 mm at Northcap University in Gurugram. Mayur Vihar received 9 mm and Jafarpur 1 mm. Data was unavailable for Najafgarh, Mehrauli, Chhatarpur and Hindon in Ghaziabad.
The rain brought a temporary improvement in Delhi’s air quality. The city’s Air Quality Index stood at 90 at 9.30 am, placing it in the ‘satisfactory’ category, according to the Central Pollution Control Board. Data on the CPCB’s SAMEER app showed 36 monitoring stations in the satisfactory category and 16 in the moderate category.
Under the CPCB scale, AQI readings from zero to 50 are classified as good, 51 to 100 as satisfactory, 101 to 200 as moderate, 201 to 300 as poor, 301 to 400 as very poor and 401 to 500 as severe. The improvement indicates how rainfall can quickly alter pollution conditions, although the source report does not establish how long the better air quality will persist.
Temperatures also fell across parts of the capital. The minimum temperature at Safdarjung was 17.2 degrees Celsius, 1.1 degrees above normal. Palam recorded 15.4 degrees Celsius, while the Ridge recorded 16.8 degrees Celsius. Lodi Road registered 18 degrees Celsius and Ayanagar 17.4 degrees Celsius. The maximum temperature was expected to settle around 27 degrees Celsius.
The continuing alert places attention on road conditions, storm-water drainage and travel across Delhi and the adjoining National Capital Region as more rain and thunderstorms remain forecast. The IMD’s next weather warning covers the immediate period following Friday morning, with heavy rainfall possible at isolated locations.

full_text:
HYDERABAD: The Telangana weather department has issued an orange warning for thunderstorms and rain in several districts, including Hyderabad, forecasting moderate rainfall accompanied by gusty winds over the next two to three hours.
According to the alert, Hyderabad, Medchal-Malkajgiri, Nalgonda, Rangareddy, Sangareddy and Yadadri-Bhuvanagiri districts are likely to receive moderate rain and moderate thunderstorms, with wind speeds of 41-61 kmph in gusts.
Light rain and thunderstorms, with gusts of less than 40 kmph, are also likely in Jangaon, Mahabubabad, Nagarkurnool, Narayanpet, Nirmal, Nizamabad, Rajanna Sircilla and Vikarabad districts during the same period.
The warning covers 14 districts in total. Residents have been advised to remain alert, particularly in areas vulnerable to waterlogging, falling branches and traffic disruptions during thunderstorms.
Hyderabad and surrounding districts face stronger winds
The forecast indicates the possibility of stronger gusts in Hyderabad and neighbouring districts compared with the other districts listed in the advisory. Commuters may experience reduced visibility and slippery roads during rainfall.
Residents are advised to:
Avoid standing under trees, electric poles and temporary structures during thunderstorms.
Stay away from open grounds, construction sites and exposed rooftops during lightning.
Avoid parking vehicles beneath trees or near hoardings.
Drive slowly, maintain a safe distance from other vehicles and avoid flooded roads.
Secure loose objects, outdoor furniture and temporary roofing.
Keep away from fallen power lines and report electrical hazards to the authorities.
The India Meteorological Department’s October 30 bulletin also lists thunderstorm and lightning warnings for Telangana, with further weather warnings indicated for the coming days.
Residents advised to monitor weather updates
People in the affected districts should follow official weather bulletins and local administration advisories. Thunderstorm activity can vary from one locality to another, and conditions may change during the warning period.
For lightning alerts, residents can also use the IMD’s Damini app, while the Mausam app provides weather forecasts and updates.
